summary:
Team CodeBusters developed DelayNet, a browser-based simulator for the Interplanetary Survival Guide challenge. It lets users experience a deep-space emergency from both sides of a delayed communication link. The crew must act while Mission Control is still waiting for the first report. By the time Earth replies, an instruction that once made sense may be dangerous.

DelayNet’s State Reconciliation Engine compares Earth’s arriving command with the original incident snapshot and the crew’s local actions. In the Coolant Cascade scenario, Earth tells the crew to open a valve after they have already vented the damaged loop. DelayNet blocks the command, explains how it could put reserve coolant at risk, and offers a simulated alternative.

The simulator uses bundled NASA/JPL Horizons data to estimate signal delays for Mars, Europa, and Titan. Students and training teams can run scenarios offline and practice checking whether delayed instructions still fit current conditions before acting.
details:
Team CodeBusters built DelayNet, a browser-based mission simulator for the Interplanetary Survival Guide challenge. It demonstrates what can happen when astronauts must respond to an emergency before Earth can advise them. By the time Mission Control’s reply arrives, the crew may have changed the conditions that made the instruction safe.

DelayNet captures a fixed snapshot as soon as an incident begins. The crew responds locally using rules for that scenario, while Mission Control works from the snapshot it receives. When Earth’s command arrives, the State Reconciliation Engine checks it against the original snapshot and the crew’s actions. In Coolant Cascade, Earth asks the crew to open a valve after they have already vented the damaged loop. DelayNet blocks the command, explains how it could put reserve coolant at risk, and offers a simulated alternative. Two other scenarios explore a power crisis and a misdiagnosis involving fictional compounds.

The creative choice was to give users three views of the same emergency. Habitat shows current conditions, Earth shows the received snapshot, and Orbit Link shows messages traveling between them. Time warp lets users see the full exchange in seconds, and a blackout control lets them test what happens when delivery is interrupted. The goal is to help students and training teams practice checking whether a delayed instruction still fits current conditions before acting.

We used NASA/JPL Horizons data to estimate signal travel times for Mars, Europa, and Titan. Bundling the data lets the demo run offline after setup. The crew and equipment readings are simulated. We designed around three constraints: Earth’s limited view of the habitat, packet timing that stays consistent when playback speed changes, and a verdict that explains why a command was blocked.

We built DelayNet with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. Zustand manages simulation state, and Dexie with IndexedDB saves checkpoints that restore the mission paused after a refresh. We tested timing and conflict rules with Vitest and deployed the static app on Antideploy. The simulator runs entirely in the browser on standard hardware.
